writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what assessment she has made of the effectiveness of the Independent Press Standards Organisation in addressing the continued publication of claims based on withdrawn millionaire migration figures; and whether she plans to take steps to require newspaper publishers to join a regulator recognised under the Royal Charter on self-regulation of the press.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
We expect all publishers to operate within the bounds of the law and adhere to high ethical and professional standards, as well as ensure appropriate routes to redress if these standards are not met. However, to protect press freedom, the UK has a self-regulatory system for the press, which is independent of government and as such the government does not intervene in or evaluate the work of regulators, including the Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO)

IPSO and the Independent Monitor of the Press (Impress) were established following the findings of the Leveson Report in 2012, to ensure these high standards are met. Complaints about misleading information in reporting can be directed to these regulators. Both IPSO and Impress enforce codes of conducts, which include clauses on accuracy, setting out the need for publishers to clearly distinguish between fact and opinion and to take care not to publish distorting or misleading information. There are no current plans to depart from this system.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what assessment she has made of the potential impact of Personal Adviser caseloads on care leavers’ safety, wellbeing and outcomes; and what steps her Department is taking to support local authorities to reduce high caseloads.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Personal Advisers play an important role in providing practical and emotional support to care leavers preparing for adulthood. They have legal duties to keep in touch with the young person and to work with them to develop a pathway plan setting out the support the local authority will provide.

Local authorities are responsible for ensuring their leaving care services have sufficient capacity and capability to meet their statutory duties. The department does not collect national data on Personal Adviser workforce numbers, caseloads, vacancies or turnover.

The department recognises evidence that high caseloads and workforce instability can reduce the time Personal Advisers have to build relationships and provide effective support for young people. We are therefore reviewing relevant statutory guidance, including considering workforce capacity, caseloads, training and professional standards, and whether greater national consistency is needed.

Ofsted has a crucial role to play in upholding children’s social care standards. They provide independent, up to date judgements on the quality of support, safeguarding and leadership, making sure children are safe and supported. Ofsted’s Inspecting Local Authority Children’s Services framework includes a standalone judgement area on the experiences and progress of care leavers. As government delivers wider reforms to the children’s social care system, Ofsted is reshaping their inspection frameworks so they continue to act as a lever for improvement.

The ‘Improving the way Ofsted inspects children’s social care’ consultation closed on 28 September 2026. Proposals included introducing a 5-point grade scale to bring more nuance to inspection grades, report cards to offer a clearer way of presenting inspection findings, and strengthening alignment with government reforms to deliver a system with a unified vision of what good looks like for children’s social care. Ofsted is analysing the consultation responses and will set out plans for 2027 onwards in due course.

The department is working closely with Ofsted to support the sector to deliver improved services and better outcomes for children, young people and families. It is for Ofsted to determine their inspection frameworks in line with government policy, including for leaving care services and care leavers.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, how many Child Maintenance Service cases involving outstanding arrears have been closed in each of the last five years because the paying parent was no longer habitually resident in the UK; and what the value of outstanding arrears was in those cases.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Child Maintenance Service (CMS) can only be used where the receiving parent, paying parent and any qualifying children are habitually resident in the UK. Where these conditions are not met, the CMS does not have jurisdiction.

Where one parent lives outside the UK, maintenance may instead be pursued through international arrangements known as the Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance Orders (REMO) process – administered by the Ministry of Justice for England and Wales, [the Scottish Government for Scotland and the Northern Ireland Executive for Northern Ireland]. Where the other parent lives in a REMO country (a country that is party to a REMO agreement with the UK), an application can be made for a child maintenance decision to be established in that country or for any UK child maintenance order to be recognised and enforced in that country.

If a paying or receiving parent moves to a country where no reciprocal maintenance agreement is in place, any outstanding arrears are not written off. They may remain recoverable by the Department for Work and Pensions if the parent subsequently returns to the UK or moves to a country where reciprocal arrangements are in place.

Where the Department determines that it no longer has jurisdiction because the paying parent is resident outside the United Kingdom, the receiving parent may be able to pursue outstanding maintenance through the Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance Orders (REMO) process if the country where the paying parent is resident has a REMO agreement with the UK, subject to the terms of that agreement.

The UK has reciprocal arrangements with a number of countries and territories.

Where the Department retains jurisdiction to calculate and collect child maintenance, it will continue to take appropriate action to secure compliance and recover outstanding arrears where necessary.

Information on the action taken in cases where a paying parent was previously within the Department’s jurisdiction but subsequently moved overseas is not held in a format that would allow it to be readily identified. Providing this information would require a manual review of individual case records and administrative systems, which could only be undertaken at disproportionate cost.

Where historic errors are identified, the Department takes appropriate corrective action, so that affected customers can be put in the position they would have been in had the original error not occurred.

writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) concluded that the available evidence no longer supports a positive benefit-risk balance for Avacopan Vifor. Its use, supply, and sale to new patients were therefore suspended from 1 September 2026, with further information available at the following link:

https://www.gov.uk/government/news/mhra-concludes-review-of-avacopan-vifor-following-reassessment-of-benefit-risk-balance

To minimise disruption to patients already receiving treatment, a six-month managed withdrawal period was put in place, during which continued supply is permitted for existing patients. The MHRA intends to revoke the United Kingdom marketing authorisation on 1 March 2027.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what criteria are applied when considering a medical waiver for an applicant diagnosed with coeliac disease.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Ministry of Defence (MOD) must find the best balance possible between allowing people with certain health conditions to join the Armed Forces, while maintaining a force that is fully deployable at short notice. Ultimately, there is an expectation that all new entrants, whether Regular or Reserve, are able to deploy anywhere in the world, to the most hostile of environments, remote from support and medical care. It is incredibly important in these environments that vital medical evacuation chains are not blocked by individuals with known medical conditions.

Gluten sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease) can only be managed by completely avoiding gluten, and failing to follow a strict gluten-free diet can lead to severe short-term symptoms and long-term health risks.

The nature of military service is such that it is not possible to guarantee an individual’s ability to self-police their diet to avoid triggers, and the ingestion of gluten can occur despite careful avoidance. There are multiple opportunities for exposure, and operational realities, whether in the UK or overseas, increases the risk of inadvertent ingestion. Environmental exposure to a trigger is not fully controllable under field conditions such as austere kitchens, ration sharing, host-nation and coalition catering, unlabelled or locally procured food.

The MOD must always put the safety, care and long-term outcome for individuals at the heart of any decision to recruit; as an employer, MOD has a legal duty of care to protect individuals and cannot knowingly, regardless of how small the risk may be, increase an individual's future risk of known complications.

Every application to join the Armed Forces is considered on a case-by-case basis by recruiting clinicians, who will make an individual assessment of the condition, its severity and the need for treatment. If an application is rejected on medical grounds, a candidate can appeal the decision providing additional medical evidence if required.

If a candidate does not meet the medical entry standards but has specialist skills that would be of exceptional benefit to the Armed Forces, the recruiting Service may consider an individually assessed waiver. This assessment does not waive the medical entry standards and there are no specific criteria relating to coeliac disease. Rather, the process allows the employing Service to exceptionally recruit someone who is below the normal entry standards; any decision to recruit someone who does not meet the normal entry standards is only made after careful assessment and will balance the need for a specific skill against medical implications and employment restrictions. For example, recruiting services may consider a waiver for candidates who possess sought after skills including but not limited to cyber, intelligence and medical skills, or individuals who are Chaplains. In these cases, a ‘skills first’ approach is prioritised rather than the traditional ‘sailor, soldier, aircrew first’ approach.

While the medical employment standards were formally reviewed in their entirety in 2024, which included a comprehensive assessment of gastrointestinal conditions, the standards do remain under constant review, with two further updates to policy being published in 2026. The standards are informed by serving medical consultants who are leaders in their respective medical fields. These consultants are experts in modern medical treatments, are up to date with emerging medical and clinical evidence and have an in depth understanding of the unique physical, cognitive and environmental demands of military service.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Justice, what steps his Department is taking to integrate statutory library and self-directed learning facilities into the design and operational specifications for (a) HMP Fosse Way and (b) other modern prison facilities.

Library and self-directed learning provision is delivered in accordance with the Prison Education and Libraries Policy Framework, which sets out the statutory duties to provide education in prisons, and requires that every prison must have a library.

Education facilities, including a library, classrooms and opportunities for self-directed learning via in-cell technology, form part of the design of all newly-built prisons.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, what steps he is taking to establish minimum standards for the provision of in-person banking services, especially in rural or hard to reach areas.
writtenQuestions.answerText:
On Monday 16 November, HM Treasury published the report of the independent Review on Access to Banking Services, chaired by Richard Lloyd OBE, which assessed how changes to banking services affect consumers. The Review considered evidence from across the UK, including the particular barriers that can affect access to banking services in rural communities.

The Government welcomes the Review and accepts the Review’s central conclusion that further action is needed. The Government intends to legislate to establish a new statutory framework that ensures reasonable access to essential in-person banking services for customers who need them, while recognising the important role of accessible digital and telephone banking.

The Government has brought forward an amendment to the Financial Services and Markets Bill to enable the creation of this framework.

In developing the detailed design of the framework, the Government will work with the Financial Conduct Authority, industry, consumer groups, and other stakeholders.

Alongside the development of the framework, the Government will work with the banking industry to deliver improvements to access to in-person banking services, so that consumers and small businesses can benefit from progress ahead of the framework coming into effect.

writtenStatements.title: Launch of the Independent Review of Culture, Accountability and Governance at the Information Commission
writtenStatements.text:
I am repeating the following Written Ministerial Statement made today in the other place by my Right Honourable Friend, the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, Lisa Nandy MP:

Today I am announcing the launch of an independent review of culture, accountability and governance at the Information Commission.

Following concerns raised about the conduct of the former Information Commissioner, the Information Commissioner’s Office commissioned an independent investigation in February 2026, which concluded in June. That investigation upheld multiple allegations against the former Commissioner and he subsequently resigned. That investigation considered the conduct of one individual but did not examine the wider organisational conditions in which the relevant events occurred. This review has therefore been established to consider those wider conditions and identify any lessons for the future. I would like to thank the former Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology, my Rt Hon Friend the Member for Leicester West, Liz Kendall, for initiating this review.

I have appointed Karon Monaghan KC to lead the review, as the independent Reviewer. As a leading employment and equality law barrister, Karon is exceptionally well placed to lead this work. She will conduct the review independently of both the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and the Information Commission, and prepare a report which will set out her findings and recommendations. I have every confidence she will conduct the review with the independence and rigour it demands.

The review comes at an important moment for the organisation, following the governance transition to the new Information Commission and the appointment of a new Board at the end of September.

The review will provide the Department and the Information Commission Board with an independent assessment of the organisation’s culture, accountability and governance arrangements, including the relationship between the Commission and DCMS, as its sponsoring department.

In particular, the review will examine cultural conditions and behavioural norms; how concerns are raised, heard, assessed and acted on; how accountability, leadership and governance arrangements operate in practice; and whether lessons can be learned from the sponsorship relationship between the Information Commission and the Department, while respecting the regulator’s independence. It will identify what should be strengthened and what should be reset, with practical, proportionate and prioritised recommendations.

I want to be clear that the review is intended to support organisational learning and improvement. It will not reopen or reinvestigate the findings of the independent investigation into the previous Information Commissioner, nor will it make findings about the conduct or performance of named individuals.

It is critically important that both current and former staff are able to contribute to the review with confidence and speak openly about their experiences, knowing that those experiences will be taken seriously. Participation will be voluntary, and the Reviewer will determine how best to engage participants.

The review is expected to report in the first quarter of 2027. I will ensure that its final report is made available to Parliament at the earliest opportunity. The report and its recommendations will also be made publicly available.

The Terms of Reference for the review, developed in consultation with the Information Commission, will be published today.
